story.title: Why should a token become permanent as soon as it is generated?
paragraphs: Ordinary autoregressive decoding commits to an output from left to right. A later phrase can make an earlier choice look wrong, but the decoder does not revise that choice in place. Asking the model to critique and regenerate its answer creates another sequential pass. Parallel decoding addresses latency, yet independently proposed tokens can also disagree with one another. COrAL studies these two problems together: how to keep the useful sequential structure while making nearby predictions revisable.

The important restriction is local. Learning arbitrary orderings over an entire sequence is difficult; COrAL instead learns dependencies within a bounded window. A target position may be predicted from an earlier prefix or reconstructed with some later text available. These are different views of the same position, and their agreement can help decide what to keep.

mechanism.title: Train for revision, then decode with several views of each position
paragraphs: The training objective has two complementary parts. Forward training predicts several future positions from clean sequences. Reconstruction training corrupts patches of a sequence and asks the model to recover the original tokens, with loss applied to corrupted positions. Patch replacement and repetition create errors that the model must learn to repair. Refinement is therefore a trained capability, rather than an instruction added to an unchanged next-token model.

Predicting different positions from one context also requires knowing which position is being queried. COrAL modifies RoPE in the final attention layer so that the query is encoded for the target position. This target-aware representation avoids a separate output head for every offset. Training is staged: adapt the last layer first, then train the network more broadly, reducing the mismatch with the pretrained model.

At inference, a sliding block contains positions to predict or revise. The model combines available conditional distributions, with weights reflecting dependency distance and context confidence. It constructs candidate blocks and verifies them using next-token and backward probabilities, with an additional contrastive term. An acceptance procedure determines how much of the block's prefix can be committed. Only that accepted prefix moves the window forward; the remaining positions can be reconsidered.

evidence.title: Accuracy and speed change with the decoding setting
paragraphs: The ablations separate two contributions. On GSM8K, the full system raises accuracy from 74.1% to 75.3% while increasing accepted-token throughput from 39.7 to 43.4 tokens/s. Removing multi-forward prediction keeps backward refinement and reaches 78.7%, but throughput falls to 14.9 tokens/s. Removing verification reaches 156.8 tokens/s, while accuracy falls to 72.4%. The 4.6-point gain and 3.9× speedup describe different operating points.

The code results expose a boundary that the headline numbers miss. HumanEval pass@1 drops from 64.6% to 13.0% with the full method, and the paper's error analysis identifies syntax as a major failure source. Disabling multi-forward prediction recovers 61.6%, at lower throughput. Local agreement is useful for refinement, but it is not enough to ensure globally well-formed programs. The experiment asks where flexible token ordering helps, and where stronger structural constraints are needed.
